name: Design a Code Assistant Backend
intent: Suggest code in an editor fast enough to feel instant, answer questions about a whole repository, and keep a company's private source code private, at a cost per developer that the business can afford.
codeTitle: debouncing with cancellation, and a context ranker
finalIntro: One pause in typing, and one question in the chat panel.
prompt: Design the backend of an assistant for software developers. In the editor it suggests the next lines of code as a developer types, and in a chat panel it answers questions about the developer's repository. Suggestions must appear quickly enough to feel instant, the assistant must know about code in the project beyond the open file, and the company's source code must stay private.
functional: Suggest a completion for the code at the cursor when the developer pauses typing
Answer questions in a chat panel using the repository's code, with links to files and lines
Keep an index of each repository and branch that the developer works on, up to date as code changes
Let the developer accept, reject or edit a suggestion, and record the choice
Respect privacy settings: files that are never sent, secrets that are removed, and code that is not kept or used for training unless the organisation allows it
nonFunctional: A completion appears about 300 ms after a typing pause at the median, and a request is abandoned after about 1 second
The editor never waits for the backend, and a request that the developer has typed past is cancelled
A chat answer starts streaming within about 2 seconds
A change on a branch is searchable in the index within about a minute
Source code is encrypted and isolated per organisation, and secrets never reach the model
The cost per active developer per day stays within a budget

firstAttempt.text: The editor extension sends the whole open file to one large model on every keystroke and shows whatever comes back as a suggestion.
limits: A request per keystroke floods the backend, and most answers arrive after the developer has typed on
A large model is slow and expensive for the short, frequent job of finishing a line
Only the open file is sent, so the assistant does not know the functions and types defined elsewhere in the project
A big file does not fit in the prompt, and the whole file is paid for again on every keystroke
Private files and secrets in the open tabs go to the model, and nobody measures whether suggestions are any good

steps.title: Debounce, cancel and set a deadline
steps.problem: A developer types several characters a second. A request per keystroke sends hundreds of requests for one line, and every answer that arrives after the next key is useless, because the text it was meant for no longer exists.
steps.fix: The editor extension waits for a short pause in typing before it asks for a completion, and sends at most one request at a time. When the developer types again, the request in flight is cancelled, and the cancellation reaches the model so that it stops spending tokens. Each request carries a deadline of about a second, and the gateway drops a request that is already too late. The completion API has a per-user rate limit as a last guard.
steps.tradeoff: Far fewer requests and no wasted answers. A longer wait before asking makes the assistant feel slower, so the pause is tuned against the model's latency: too short and nothing is saved, too long and the answer arrives after the developer has moved on.

steps.title: Build a small, relevant context
steps.problem: The model only knows what is in the prompt. The open file alone misses the types and functions defined elsewhere, and sending everything does not fit the window and costs a lot on every request.
steps.fix: A context builder assembles the prompt from the most useful pieces within a token budget: the code before and after the cursor, the definitions of the symbols used nearby, recently edited files, other open tabs and similar code from the project. Each piece has a priority. The builder takes pieces in priority order, skips those that do not fit, and keeps the order stable so that the start of the prompt repeats from one request to the next.
steps.tradeoff: The model sees what it needs in a short prompt, which is faster and cheaper. Choosing the pieces is a heuristic that can miss the one that matters, so the choices are measured, and the budget is a setting that can be tuned.

steps.title: Index the repository
steps.problem: The assistant must find relevant code anywhere in a large repository, in chat and in completions, and the code changes all day and differs between branches.
steps.fix: Repository events go onto a queue. An indexer splits changed files into chunks along their syntax (functions, classes, blocks), hashes each chunk, and embeds only the chunks whose hash is new. The index holds the vectors, a keyword index and a table of symbols, and it is kept per repository and per branch as a small layer on top of the main branch, so that a branch switch means choosing another layer. Chat searches it with the question's embedding and with keywords, and cites the files and lines it used.
steps.tradeoff: Relevant code is found across the whole project, and an edit is searchable within about a minute. The index is another system to run and keep fresh, and files that the developer has just edited are not in it yet, so the open files are read from the editor directly.

steps.title: Two paths: completion and chat
steps.problem: Finishing a line and answering a question about the architecture are different jobs. One model and one budget is too slow for the first and too small for the second.
steps.fix: Completion goes to a small, fast model with a short context and a tight deadline, and its answer is streamed straight to the editor. Chat goes to a larger model with retrieved code, a longer deadline and more tokens, and streams its answer with citations. A router picks the path from the request type, and can send a hard completion to the larger model when the developer asks for more.
steps.tradeoff: Each path is tuned for its own latency and cost, and most of the traffic, which is completions, uses the cheap model. Two paths mean two models to evaluate and keep up to date.

steps.title: Cache and share repeated work
steps.problem: Every request repeats a long start that is almost the same as the last one: the instructions and the same files. Paying for those tokens again and again is most of the bill.
steps.fix: The service keeps the beginning of the prompt stable, with fixed instructions first, then the repository context, then the code near the cursor, so that the serving layer can reuse the work already done for that prefix. The prefix cache is keyed by organisation and repository, and is never shared across organisations. Identical requests that arrive together are merged into one.
steps.tradeoff: Cost and latency fall noticeably, as only the changing end of the prompt is processed afresh. Cached context must be invalidated when files change, and the cache must never mix organisations, so its key and its lifetime are part of the security design.

steps.title: Keep the code private and the model safe
steps.problem: The prompt contains source code, and source code contains secrets. Files in the repository can also contain text that tries to give the model instructions, such as a comment that says to send the environment to a web address.
steps.fix: A filter runs between the context builder and the model. It drops files that match the organisation's exclusion rules (environment files, keys, certificates, folders marked as private), scans what is left for secrets by pattern and by entropy, and removes them. Code is encrypted at rest and in transit, isolated per organisation, not logged by default, and kept only as long as the retention policy says. Text found in the repository is treated as data, and the assistant cannot take actions, so an injected comment cannot make it do anything.
steps.tradeoff: A leak needs several controls to fail, and the organisation can show what is stored and for how long. Filters drop some useful context and can miss a novel secret format, so they are tested with planted secrets, and the assistant is given no tools that could send data out.

steps.title: Measure whether it helps
steps.problem: A suggestion can be fluent and useless, or subtly wrong. Without measurement the team cannot tell whether a change to the context, the model or the prompt made anything better.
steps.fix: The extension records what happened to each suggestion: shown, accepted, edited after accepting or dismissed, and the latency at each stage, without storing the code unless the organisation allows it. Dashboards track the acceptance rate and the share of accepted code that is later deleted. An offline set of tasks, such as a hidden function body that a test suite checks, scores each model and context change before release, and new versions go to a small share of developers first. A cheap syntax check drops a suggestion that cannot parse before it is shown.
steps.tradeoff: Changes are judged on evidence, and a bad release is caught on a few developers. Acceptance is an imperfect measure, since people accept things they later fix, so it is read together with the offline results and the share of accepted code that stays.

failures.scenario: A request per keystroke floods the backend at the start of the workday
failures.impact: Thousands of developers start typing at once, the queue grows, and completions arrive seconds late or not at all, which also slows chat.
failures.answer: Debounce and cancellation cut most requests at the source. A per-user rate limit and a deadline at the gateway shed what is left: a request that cannot finish in time is dropped, and the editor shows nothing rather than something stale. Completion and chat have separate capacity, so that one cannot starve the other.

failures.scenario: The index is stale after a branch switch or a large merge
failures.impact: Chat cites functions that were renamed or no longer exist on the developer's branch, and completions call old signatures.
failures.answer: The index is kept per branch as a layer over the main branch, and chunks are identified by content hash, so a switch selects another layer and only changed chunks are re-embedded. Files open in the editor are always read live, and the chat answer says when the index is behind. A merge is applied as a batch of changed hashes, with progress visible.

failures.scenario: A secret in an open file reaches the model
failures.impact: An API key in an environment file, open in a tab, is placed in a prompt and sent to a third-party model, and may be logged.
failures.answer: Exclusion rules keep such files out of the context, a secret scanner removes what the rules miss, and nothing is logged by default. A test suite plants known secrets in sample repositories and fails the release if any appears in a prompt. The model provider's retention and training terms are part of the contract, and the organisation can see them.

failures.scenario: A suggestion does not compile, or imports a package that does not exist
failures.impact: The developer accepts it, loses minutes finding the error, and trust in the assistant falls. A non-existent package name could even be registered by an attacker.
failures.answer: A fast syntax check drops completions that cannot parse, and imports are checked against the project's lockfile and installed packages, so that a name that is not there is not suggested as if it were. The share of accepted suggestions that are edited or deleted soon after is tracked as a quality signal, and offline tests with a real compiler score each release.

alternatives.title: How to find relevant code for a completion

options.name: Only the open files and recent edits
options.pro: Fast, simple, no index to build, and always current
options.con: Misses the types and functions defined elsewhere in the project

options.name: Embedding search over the repository
options.pro: Finds related code by meaning, even when names differ
options.con: Needs an index that is kept fresh, adds latency, and can return similar but wrong code

options.name: Symbol-aware lookup, using the language's definitions and references
options.pro: Precise: the exact signature of what is being called
options.con: Needs support for each language and a working build or language server

alternatives.pick: Open files plus symbol definitions for completions, where speed and precision matter, and embedding and keyword search for chat, where recall matters more than latency.

alternatives.title: Where the index lives

options.name: On the developer's machine
options.pro: The code never leaves the laptop, and it is always the local state
options.con: Heavy on the laptop, built again on every machine, and no sharing between developers

options.name: On the server, per organisation
options.pro: One index for the team, built once and searched fast
options.con: Source code is stored on a server, so isolation, encryption and retention must be right

options.name: Both: a local index for the open work, a server index for the rest
options.pro: Fresh for the files being edited, shared for the rest of the repository
options.con: Two indexes to merge at query time

alternatives.pick: A server index per organisation, layered by branch, plus live reading of the open files from the editor. Organisations with strict rules can choose a local-only mode with weaker chat.

alternatives.title: One model or two

options.name: One large model for everything
options.pro: One thing to evaluate and run
options.con: Too slow for completions and far too costly for the many short requests

options.name: A small model for completions and a larger one for chat
options.pro: Each is tuned for its own latency and cost
options.con: Two models to evaluate, update and route between

options.name: A small model first, escalating to a larger one when the developer asks for more
options.pro: Cheap by default, and capable when needed
options.con: Needs a clear signal for escalation, and the second try costs extra time

alternatives.pick: A small model for completions and a larger one for chat, with escalation on request. Completions are most of the traffic, so the small model sets the bill.

quiz.question: The completion backend is overloaded. Logs show one request per keystroke, and most answers arrive after the developer has typed more. What is the best change?
options: Add more servers behind the gateway, since a bigger fleet will return every answer in time
Show answers from the previous request while the new one is on its way, so that the editor never looks empty
Wait for a short pause in typing before asking, send one request at a time, and cancel it when the developer types again
Send each request to two models, and use whichever answer arrives first for the suggestion
quiz.explanation: Most requests are for text that no longer exists by the time the answer arrives. Debouncing and cancelling remove them at the source, and cancelling stops the model from spending tokens on them. More servers and duplicate requests increase the cost, and showing old answers shows suggestions for text that has changed.

quiz.question: A developer switches to a feature branch where a function was renamed. Chat still cites the old name from the main branch. What is the best fix?
options: Keep the index per branch as a layer over the main branch, re-embed only changed chunks, and read open files live from the editor
Rebuild the whole index of the repository every time any developer switches branch
Tell the model in the prompt that the branch may differ, and let it decide which name is current
Index only the main branch, since feature branches are temporary and usually small
quiz.explanation: A per-branch layer on top of the main index means a switch selects another layer, and hashes identify the few chunks that changed. Rebuilding everything is slow and costly, the model cannot know which name is current, and ignoring branches gives wrong answers for most of the developer's day.

quiz.question: An environment file with an API key is open in an editor tab, and the assistant sends open tabs as context. What is the most reliable control?
options: Add a line to the prompt asking the model never to repeat any secret that it sees in the context
Tell developers not to keep secrets in files that they have open while the assistant is on
Send only the first 20 lines of each open tab, since secrets are usually near the end of a file
Exclude such files by rule, scan what remains for secrets before sending, and test the release with planted secrets
quiz.explanation: The secret must not reach the model at all, so the control sits before the model: exclusion rules, a scanner and a test that fails if a planted secret appears in a prompt. A request to the model does not stop data leaving, and policies for people or a guess about where secrets are will miss cases.
